tasks.desc: Implement the complete Python program: parse input, build l/r/sign, compute earliest later bad partner via backward same-left/right scan and four sign/original-mirrored crossing sweeps using a segment tree over right endpoints with min-heaps of left endpoints, combine partners, build suffix minima, and answer queries.

Verify correctness and performance: run the provided samples, and run a separate small random brute-force difference-constraints checker (including touching endpoints, opposite-sign crossings, and duplicate reversed intervals) to confirm the pairwise bad-pair characterization and debug any mismatches.

If the pairwise certificate is disproved or the implementation is too slow, switch to a different approach (offline descending 2D range minimum or sliding-window dynamic conflict maintenance) and re-verify.

proposals: Implement the earliest-bad-pair approach first: backward scans for same left/right endpoints, two mirrored same-sign crossing sweeps using a segment tree over right endpoints with per-right min-heaps of left endpoints, then suffix minima to answer queries. Pitfall to watch: strict open ranges, per-sign separation, and not treating right-left endpoint touching as bad.

Try the sliding-window approach as a fallback: maintain a dynamic active set and a conflict counter; endpoint conflicts by counts, crossing conflicts by dynamic 2D range counting. Pitfall: 2D dynamic counting is heavy and crossing counts need 64-bit arithmetic.

Consider an offline descending-index 2D range-minimum method: insert later intervals into a 2D segment tree storing minimum index and query the two crossing rectangles for each earlier interval. Pitfall: memory and implementation complexity of 2D range minimum.

Consider CDQ divide-and-conquer or parallel binary search on the index to find earliest bad partners. Pitfall: higher asymptotic cost and subtle management of already-found partners or 3D dominance predicates.

Use Mo’s algorithm or direct difference-constraints checking only for small-scale verification or as a last resort. Pitfall: too slow for full constraints due to many updates or per-query graph construction.
next: Implement the complete Python program for the pairwise-bad-pair solution and verify it. Use l=min(S,T), r=max(S,T), sign=0 if S<T else 1. Compute the earliest later bad partner for each person: (1) backward scan for same l or same r; (2) for same-sign crossing, run an increasing-index sweep for each sign on original coordinates and on mirrored coordinates (l'=N+1-r, r'=N+1-l). In each sweep maintain a segment tree over right endpoints where each leaf is a min-heap of encoded (left,index) for active earlier intervals of that sign; for current interval [L,R], extract all active earlier intervals with L < r_i < R and l_i < L, set their crossing partner to the current index, then insert the current interval. Take the elementwise minimum of all partner sources, build a suffix minimum, and answer query [L,R] with Yes iff suffix[L] > R. Use strict open ranges, separate signs, and test on both samples plus a separate small random brute-force difference-constraints checker that includes touching endpoints.
